measurements.notes: THE HEADLINE, AND IT DEFLATES THE SYNTHETIC RESULT: over 16 real sites the structured view costs 1397 tokens on average against 1366 for one CSS-resolution viewport screenshot. RE-MEASURED under the hardened distiller v2 (shadow DOM + iframes + [pixels] bg + mark lines, from the Linux round-3 audit); the figures below are the post-hardening ones. STATE THE AGGREGATION EXPLICITLY, because the two defensible summaries disagree and the difference is not cosmetic: the ratio of TOTALS (22354 structured tokens vs 16x1366) is 0.98x — the structured view is very slightly MORE expensive than screenshotting each viewport once — while the MEAN of per-site ratios is 1.27x and the MEDIAN is 1.15x. The mean-of-ratios is biased upward because a site where structure is 3x cheaper contributes as much as one where it is 2x more expensive, despite costing a fraction of the tokens. The ratio of totals is the number to quote for 'what does a browsing session cost'; the median is the number to quote for 'what does a typical page cost'. Neither is the 3.49x measured on the synthetic duel pages. Structure wins on 10/16 sites. The reason is structural and worth stating plainly in any paper: a screenshot has a FLAT cost that depends only on the viewport, while a structured view scales with information density. So the ratio is not a property of the method, it is a property of the page. Range 0.46x (Hacker News: 2963 tokens of pure text, the structured view costs TWICE a screenshot) to 3.11x (Vercel: 439 tokens, a sparse marketing page). By category: vitrine 2.20x, webapp-canvas 1.74x, presse 1.21x, reference 0.93x, media 0.97x, commerce 0.83x, webapp 0.78x. COST OF THE HARDENING, attributed rather than assumed: total structured tokens rose 21766 -> 22354 (+2.7%), but only part of that is the distiller. Four sites were byte-stable across the two runs (Apple, Stripe, Vercel, YouTube home: 0 token delta), which shows the harness is deterministic; Wikipedia's +127 is explained by its 13 new `mark` lines (colour-only semantics) and MDN's +273 by 1 mark + 2 [pixels] bg plus ad churn; GitHub (+109) and Hacker News (+46) emitted ZERO new line kinds, so their delta is live-site churn between runs, not the distiller. Honest read: declaring the four extra content classes costs roughly 1-2% on real pages — the completeness is close to free. One expectation refuted: YouTube, the archetypal Polymer app, was predicted to explode under shadow-DOM recursion and moved 0 tokens. Probing it directly: 533 custom elements, ZERO with an open shadowRoot — YouTube's components render into light DOM, so a plain TreeWalker already saw everything. Closed shadow roots would be a genuine surviving blind spot (element.shadowRoot returns null and the content is neither read nor declared); we did not find one in this battery, and a router cannot detect them, so it remains an open risk to state rather than a measured failure. Structure wins on visually rich / semantically sparse pages and LOSES on text-dense ones — which is the opposite of the intuition that 'text is cheap'. Two corrections in favour of the structured side, both real: (a) a viewport screenshot only shows one screen, and covering a whole page took 7.6 screens on average (19 on Stripe and Amazon), so the whole-page comparison is 1.31x with the naive whole-document view and much better if the router only ever needs one screen; (b) at Retina 2x the screenshot costs 4784 tokens on a high-res model, moving the average ratio to 4.54x — but only 1534 on a legacy-tier model (1.46x), because the API downscales before charging. 6/16 sites raised a consent banner (Stripe, Vercel, YouTube, BBC, Amazon.fr, leboncoin), which a router must dismiss before the view means anything — it is the single most common real-web obstacle we hit, ahead of any rendering issue.

Meanwhile the screen behind it is dense: content energy 0.691 for the window, 0.876 measured over the tab group's own rect. So a router asking the only question it can ask — 'how much of this client area does structure account for?' — gets 89.4% and concludes the window is well described.
